clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant renal magnesium-wasting disorder caused by variants in FXYD2, encoding the gamma-subunit of the sodium-potassium ATPase
The biochemical signature is hypomagnesaemia accompanied by hypocalciuria, mirroring the pattern seen in Gitelman syndrome
Presentation is often mild, with fatigue, muscle cramps, or an incidental low magnesium, though childhood convulsions have been described
Unlike FHHNC, there is no nephrocalcinosis, hypercalciuria, or progressive renal impairment
A recurrent dominant-negative variant affecting the gamma-subunit accounts for many reported families
Management is long-term oral magnesium supplementation, titrated to relieve symptoms rather than to fully normalise serum levels
Consider the diagnosis in autosomal dominant hypomagnesaemia with hypocalciuria and confirm with FXYD2 testing
reference.pathophysiology: The gamma-subunit encoded by FXYD2 modulates the activity of the basolateral sodium-potassium ATPase in the distal convoluted tubule, the main site of active transcellular magnesium reabsorption. A dominant-negative variant impairs correct routing or function of the ATPase, reducing the electrochemical gradient that drives apical magnesium entry through TRPM6. The result is defective distal magnesium reabsorption and renal magnesium wasting. As in Gitelman syndrome, reduced distal tubular sodium chloride handling promotes compensatory proximal sodium and calcium reabsorption, producing the associated hypocalciuria. Because the defect is confined to distal magnesium handling, calcium deposition and progressive nephron loss do not occur.
additionalInvestigations: Serum magnesium with fractional excretion of magnesium confirming renal loss
Spot urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio demonstrating hypocalciuria
Serum potassium and venous blood gas to distinguish from Gitelman syndrome
Family biochemical screening consistent with dominant inheritance
redFlags: Symptomatic hypomagnesaemia causing seizures or tetany
Profound hypomagnesaemia with secondary hypocalcaemia and cardiac irritability
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally benign with a normal life expectancy and preserved renal function; symptoms are controlled with lifelong magnesium supplementation, though complete biochemical correction is often not achievable.
pitfalls: Assuming a Gitelman-like biochemical picture excludes an FXYD2 cause
Attempting to fully normalise serum magnesium and provoking diarrhoea with high oral doses
Overlooking a dominant family history that points to the diagnosis
Attributing symptoms solely to concurrent medication such as proton-pump inhibitors
references: OMIM entry for isolated dominant hypomagnesaemia
management: Lifelong oral magnesium supplementation, titrated to relieve symptoms rather than to fully normalise serum magnesium
Use of better-tolerated organic magnesium salts in divided intake to limit diarrhoea and improve absorption
Correction of symptomatic hypomagnesaemia during acute decompensation, with parenteral magnesium if severe or accompanied by tetany or seizures
Periodic monitoring of serum magnesium and symptom control, with renal ultrasound reassurance that nephrocalcinosis does not develop
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and biochemical screening of at-risk family members
Nephrology or clinical genetics referral to confirm the FXYD2 diagnosis and guide long-term care
